nodes.title: Note: MiniMax H3
widgets_values:
## MiniMax H3

[MiniMax H3](https://www.minimax.io/blog/minimax-h3) is MiniMax's general-purpose, omni-modal generation model. It jointly understands text, image, video, and audio, and generates video with **native stereo audio**: voice, sound effects, and music are modeled jointly in a single forward pass, not layered on afterward. Output is up to 2K resolution, 24fps, and up to about 15 seconds.

## ComfyUI links
- [ComfyUI#15224](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/pull/15224)
- [🤗 Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3)

## About this workflow

This template runs the **reference-to-video (ref2va)** task using the `MiniMaxH3ReferenceToVideo` node. It takes any mix of reference images, videos, and standalone audio, and weaves them into the generation to lock in a character's identity, a style, a motion, a camera move, or a voice.

**Key inputs**

- **ref_images / ref_videos / ref_video_audios / ref_audios**: up to 9 reference images, 3 reference videos (each may carry its own paired soundtrack), and 3 standalone reference audio clips
- **prompt**: reference the inputs by tag, in the exact order they were connected, for example `<Picture 1>`, `<Video 1>`, `<Audio 1>`, then describe the target scene, motion, and audio
- **ref_image_size**: `match` scales references down to the generation's resolution (faster); `max` keeps up to a 2048px short edge for stronger identity fidelity, at the cost of speed since reference tokens ride along every sampling step
- **width / height**: set via Resolution Selector.
- **duration (seconds)**: converted to a valid frame `length` by the Math Expression node

**Sampling and decode**

- Sampler: `res_multistep`. `beta` or `normal` scheduler tends to outperform `simple` for reference-heavy prompts like this one
- The sampler's joint audio+video `LATENT` output feeds directly into both `VAEDecode` (video, `minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16`) and `VAEDecodeAudio` (audio, `minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32`); each decode node automatically pulls its own half out of the packed latent. `CreateVideo` then muxes the two into a single MP4 with synced sound
- The diffusion model here is `minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors`, a different set of weights from the `fl2va` model used by the t2v/i2v templates

Ref2va's output is very sensitive to prompt wording; matching the reference tags precisely and being explicit about which reference drives which part of the shot tends to work best.

**vae**

- [minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3/resolve/main/vae/minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors)
- [minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3/resolve/main/vae/minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors)

**diffusion_models**

- [minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3/resolve/main/diffusion_models/minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors)

**text_encoders**

- [qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3/resolve/main/text_encoders/qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors)

**loras**

- 4 steps: [minimax_h3_ref2v_turbo_4step_v0.1_comfyui_bf16.safetensors](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3/resolve/main/loras/minimax_h3_ref2v_turbo_4step_v0.1_comfyui_bf16.safetensors)

**embeddings**

- [10 style embeddings](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3/tree/main/embeddings) (`minimaxh3_*.safetensors`), for example `minimaxh3_art_is_explosion`

## Model Storage Location

```
📂 ComfyUI/
├── 📂 models/
│   ├── 📂 vae/
│   │   ├── minimax_h3_video_vae_fp16.safetensors
│   │   └── minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors
│   ├── 📂 diffusion_models/
│   │   └── minimax_h3_ref2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors
│   ├── 📂 text_encoders/
│   │   └── qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors
│   ├── 📂 loras/
│   │   └── minimax_h3_ref2v_turbo_4step_v0.1_comfyui_bf16.safetensors
│   └── 📂 embeddings/
│       └── minimaxh3_art_is_explosion.safetensors
```

## Using Prompt Embeddings

Prompt embeddings (supported since [ComfyUI#15697](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/pull/15697)) add reusable style tokens to your prompt. Download one or more embeddings from the folder above into `ComfyUI/models/embeddings/`, then reference one in the prompt text with the `embedding:` prefix and the filename without its extension, for example:

`embedding:minimaxh3_art_is_explosion`

Using an embedding is optional and the template runs fine without one.

## Report Issue

Note: Please update ComfyUI first ([guide](https://docs.comfy.org/installation/update_comfyui)) and prepare required models. Desktop/Cloud updates follow stable releases, so some nightly-supported models may not be available yet.

- Cannot run / runtime errors: [ComfyUI/issues](https://github.com/comfyanonymous/ComfyUI/issues)
- UI / frontend issues: [ComfyUI_frontend/issues](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI_frontend/issues)
- Workflow issues: [workflow_templates/issues](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/workflow_templates/issues)

subject_definitions:

<Subject 1> is the solid alien planet constructed from <Picture 1>, preserving its coherent spherical shape, blue-purple geography, cratered cellular terrain, recognizable land and basin layout, and overall planetary scale. Do not reproduce the reference image's captions, borders, inset panels, or additional planet views.

<Subject 2> is the planet's thin atmosphere and its two major cyclone systems from <Picture 1>. One cyclone is above the equator on the upper-left hemisphere and one is below the equator on the lower-left hemisphere. The dark water basin between them is a fixed surface feature. Thry rotate very slightly.

<Subject 3> is the cyan auroral curtain from <Picture 1>, located in the upper atmosphere above the equatorial orbital band. It consists of translucent vertical rays and rapidly, dramatically shifting and folding luminous curtains.

<Subject 4> is the cyan-teal surface-light network from <Picture 1>, located below the equatorial orbital band and fixed precisely to the nightside terrain. Its branch geometry, node positions, lighting, and terrain alignment remain static.

<Subject 5> is the thin equatorial orbital-infrastructure band from <Picture 1>, composed of extremely small, discontinuous artificial lights and structures. It is separate from the atmosphere and surface, not a solid ring, and does not move as one rigid object.

<Subject 6> is the distant relativistic impactor cue. It is one unresolved hard white point, very softly and intermittently strobing, just barely visible in isolated black space above and to the right of the planet. Only one point exists at any instant. It has no trail, exhaust, flare rays, continuous glow, or readable vehicle form.

<Subject 7> is the hidden far-side impact light and expanding optical bloom. The physical impact occurs behind the fixed upper-right planetary horizon and remains fully occulted by <Subject 1>. Its visible result is a compact white-blue off-limb flash, a narrow growing blue-white atmospheric backlight hugging the local limb, brief relighting of the nearby rim and cloud tops, and a smooth source-driven bloom that expands outward from that same fixed hidden impact location until the frame saturates to white.

summary:

[reference generation] The target video is a single continuous five-second orbital shot. <Subject 1> appears calm, inhabited, and visually active through subtle atmospheric circulation, moving aurora, static surface infrastructure, and restrained orbital traffic. <Subject 6> briefly and softly strobes as a tiny incoming point, disappears behind the upper-right horizon, and is followed by <Subject 7>. A hidden impact source creates a growing blue-white backlight behind the upper-right limb, then expands into a source-driven white-blue bloom that overtakes the image. No physical aftermath is shown.

retention_analysis:

<Subject 1> (appears throughout [Shot 1] until total saturation): fully_preserved - the same planet, geography, terrain, orientation, and scale remain stable before the flash.

<Subject 2> (appears before saturation in [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - both cyclone centers remain fixed while separate cloud layers circulate slowly.

<Subject 3> (appears before saturation in [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - the aurora remains above the orbital band and visibly active through independent filament motion.

<Subject 4> (appears before saturation in [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - the surface-light network remains below the orbital band and geometrically locked to the terrain.

<Subject 5> (appears before saturation in [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - the orbital band remains thin, delicate, equatorial, and subtly active through a few independent moving or flickering points.

<Subject 6> (appears briefly before the impact in [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - the impactor remains one small, softly strobing point, just barely visible, and is never duplicated or stretched into a trail.

<Subject 7> (appears during the final phase of [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - the hidden impact remains fixed behind the upper-right horizon and produces a compact off-limb flash, a local growing atmospheric backlight, and a smooth expanding white-blue bloom that overtakes the frame.

detailed_description:

The target video uses photorealistic scientific-cinematic deep-space photography. It contains one inertially locked composition, one living planet, one distant impactor cue, one hidden far-side impact, and no visible aftermath.

[Shot 1] <Subject 1> fills approximately seventy-five percent of the frame height and sits left of center. Its upper-right limb is positioned near the center-right of the composition, leaving open black space beyond it. The camera is completely locked with no pan, push, zoom, orbit, roll, or shake.

<Subject 2> shows restrained atmospheric depth. Both cyclone eyes and their overall spiral geometry remain stable. Thin outer cloud bands drift slowly across fixed terrain, high-altitude wisps circulate subtly around each eye, and cloud-top brightness changes create gentle differential motion. The southern cyclone does not rotate faster than the northern cyclone. The dark basin between them remains fixed.

<Subject 3> is continuously active. Slow waves travel laterally along the lower auroral boundary. Separate vertical cyan rays brighten, lengthen, retract, dim, and fold while the curtain remains magnetically organized above the atmosphere.

<Subject 4> remains completely terrain-registered. Its hard-edged teal branches, nodes, alignment, and shape never move or deform. Only very slight local brightness variation is visible. It does not ripple with <Subject 3>.

<Subject 5> shows restrained activity. Most of the equatorial orbital band remains nearly stationary at this scale, but two or three individual hard silver-white points brighten independently and drift subtly along the equatorial path. One tiny point disappears behind the planetary limb. The whole band never flows, pulses, or rotates as one rigid object.

From approximately 00:00.100 to 00:01.250, <Subject 6> appears only as one tiny hard white point in the isolated upper-right black space. It briefly flashes on, switches completely off, then briefly flashes on once more slightly closer to the upper-right horizon. Each appearance is very small, faint, and brief. No visible light connects the appearances. Only one point is visible at any instant.

The final flash of <Subject 6> disappears fully behind the planet. Only a short empty interval follows.

At approximately 00:01.450, <Subject 7> begins as a compact white-blue flash from one fixed location just beyond the upper-right horizon. The physical impact site remains fully hidden behind the planet.

Immediately after the flash, a narrow blue-white atmospheric backlight appears behind the local upper-right limb. It hugs the curvature of the atmosphere and remains confined to the impact longitude. This off-limb glow broadens gradually around a short section of the limb and expands outward into the surrounding black space, while remaining clearly sourced from the same hidden point behind the planet.

The backlight then transitions into a smooth photographic bloom. The bloom expands outward from the hidden impact location, first overloading the nearby atmospheric rim and adjacent cloud tops, then progressively lifting the exposure across the visible hemisphere. The right side of the frame and the impact-facing limb brighten first. More distant regions brighten later.

The growing blue-white glow remains local to the impact side. It does not race around the full planetary circumference, does not become a complete luminous shell, and does not create a persistent starburst, ejecta fan, plume, shock ring, or orange fireball. The source remains hidden, and the bloom remains clearly driven from that fixed upper-right impact site.

<Subject 4> does not cause the relighting. It remains a fixed emitted-light network and gradually becomes less distinct as ambient illumination and bloom intensity increase. <Subject 5> remains spatially fixed and also becomes less distinct under the growing exposure.

Any moon that remains in frame stays visually secondary and does not develop a separate mirrored flare or its own independent impact-side bloom before the final whiteout.

By approximately 00:04.100, the bloom has expanded enough that the planet, stars, atmosphere, aurora, surface network, and orbital band are nearly overwhelmed. By approximately 00:04.400, the frame is complete uniform featureless white. Full white holds through the final frame. Do not reveal ejecta, shockwaves, fires, crater geometry, grid failure, atmosphere loss, or orbital damage in this clip.

overall_soundscape:

Faint electronic observation noise and restrained telemetry are audible before impact. The first horizon flash produces one dry electronic clipping snap followed by a brief harsh broadband sensor overload. The overload continues into the whiteout and provides a continuous audio seam for the next clip. No dialogue, engine noise, explosion boom, orchestral hit, rhythmic pulse, or sustained low cinematic rumble.

non_diegetic_music:

N/A
